explanation:
The `utime` and `utimes` system calls are used to manually change the access time (atime) and modification time (mtime) stored within the inode of the file specified by `filename`. These calls are crucial for maintaining file integrity or performing backups where original timestamps must be preserved.

Historically, `utime(2)` provided time specification using `struct utimbuf`, offering second resolution using `time_t` fields (`actime` and `modtime`). The preferred function, `utimes(2)`, offers higher precision, utilizing an array of two `struct timeval` structures to achieve microsecond resolution. In the `utimes` call, the array `times[0]` specifies the new access time, and `times[1]` specifies the new modification time. Unlike `atime` and `mtime`, the status change time (`ctime`) is automatically updated to the current time whenever these syscalls are successfully executed, regardless of whether the other timestamps actually change.

If the `times` argument is passed as `NULL` to either function, both the access and modification times of the file are automatically set to the current system time at the moment of the call.

Changing timestamps is subject to permission checks. A process is allowed to change timestamps if: 1) the process has appropriate privileges (e.g., superuser); 2) the effective user ID of the process matches the user ID of the file owner; or 3) if the `times` argument is `NULL`, the process only needs write permission for the file. Failures often result in `EACCES` (permission denied) or `ENOENT` (file not found).

Both functions return 0 upon successful execution. On error, they return -1, and the global variable `errno` is set to indicate the cause of the failure. Common errors include `EPERM` (operation not permitted), `EACCES` (search permission denied on a component of the path prefix), and `EFAULT` (bad address).

Modern applications are generally encouraged to use the newer `utimensat(2)` interface, which supports nanosecond precision and the ability to specify times relative to an open file descriptor, avoiding potential race conditions.
keywords: utime, utimes, timestamp, access time, modification time, atime, mtime, ctime, file time, utimensat, timeval, utimbuf, file system
example_explanation: This C example creates a temporary file and uses `utimes` to set its access time to one hour prior and its modification time to 30 minutes prior, demonstrating the use of the `struct timeval` array for precise time control.
